title: Robust Electroreduction of CO2 at a Poly(4-vinylpyridine)– Copper Electrode
abstract: Electrocatalytic synthesis of specialty chemicals or fuels from CO2 using alternative energy is a promising approach for reducing our carbon footprint and our dependence on fossil fuels. The main roadblock towards the commercialization of this technology is the absence of a sustainable catalytic system. To comply with the sustainable chemistry principles, this system has to employ low-toxicity or nontoxic earth-abundant materials as catalysts and water as a solvent, while operating at mild conditions (atmospheric CO2 pressures and near room temperatures). Unfortunately, among the metals that are sufficiently active in CO2 electroreduction, [1c, 2] only Sn and Cu meet the sustainable chemistry criteria. Tin is “specialized” in the synthesis of formate, owing to its inability to dissociate the C¢O bonds. Copper is unique, as it can synthetize C1+ hydrocarbons and oxygenates such as ethylene, ethane, ethanol, and propanol. However, the performance of these two metals is plagued by large overpotentials (ca. ¢1 V), fast deactivation, and, in the case of Cu, low selectivity. The large overpotentials and low selectivity emanate from the thermodynamic and kinetic challenges of CO2 reduction. [1a] The fast deactivation is mostly caused by electrode poisoning from heavy-metal contaminants, which are typical of conventional electrolytes. In addition, the electrode surface can be modified by cathodic corrosion, such as dissolution/re-precipitation and poisoned by reaction products such as carbon, which is poorly understood. Although the robustness of the electrocatalyst is as important as its energy efficiency and current density, prior research efforts have mainly focused on the improvement of the latter two properties. The main design principles implemented so far in this area include (nano)structuring and/or oxidation of metal surfaces. Although this approach has proven to be very efficient, it is intrinsically incapable of protecting the electrodes from deactivation by heavy metals and corrosion, and a mitigating technique such as addition of water-soluble chelating agents to the electrolyte does not work for copper. In this context, it is critical to develop a new class of material that is, by design, more robust and catalytically active than metals. Such an emerging class includes materials based on Ndoped sp carbon, including N-heteroaromatic organic compounds and N-doped graphitic carbon. 7] In fact, N-doped carbon nanotubes (N-CNTs) are only marginally inferior in formate synthesis to nano-Sn on graphene. Much lower overpotentials of approximately ¢0.35 V are required to produce formate through electropolymerized phthalocyanine complexes of Ni and Co, although the faradaic efficiencies of these electrocatalysts is unclear. Electropolymerized pyridine complexes of Cr, Co, and Fe convert CO2 to formaldehyde in 0.1 m NaClO4 at ¢1.1 V (Ag/AgCl) with faradaic efficiencies of 87, 39, and 28 %, respectively. Interestingly, water-soluble N-heterocycles and N-heterocycle-based ionic liquids stabilize Sn electrodes, with increasing current density and decreasing overpotential in the formate synthesis. 11] Given these data, along with the well-documented catalytic activity of metal complexes of macrocycles with pyridyl ligands, 12] we were curious to test the effect of N-heteroaromatic polymers on the catalytic activity of metals. These polymers have not yet been employed as a building block in CO2 electrocatalysts. The exception is the incorporation of cobalt The development of efficient and robust catalysts based on earth-abundant and nontoxic materials is critical for the viability of the electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 into useful chemicals. Herein, we report a new class of electrocatalysts with incorporated mechanisms of their stabilization. A Cu electrode coated with a poly(4-vinyl pyridine) film synthesizes formate at a faradaic efficiency of 40 % at an overpotential of ¢0.67 V, and its catalytic activity does not degrade after 30 h of operation. We attribute the outstanding catalytic properties of the new hybrid material to the formation of Cu–polymer complexes, as well as to new intrinsic mechanisms of the electrode stabilization offered by the N-heteroaromatic polymer. This is the first report of CO2 electroreduction with copper–N-heteroaromatic ligand complexes. More generally, our study offers a new simple strategy to design and prepare robust CO2 reduction electrocatalysts based on earth-abundant metals.

sections.heading: Robust Electroreduction of CO2 at a Poly(4-vinylpyridine)– Copper Electrode
sections.text: Sathish Ponnurangam, Chang Min Yun, and Irina V. Chernyshova*[a]

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrocatalytic synthesis of specialty chemicals or fuels from
CO2 using alternative energy is a promising approach for reducing our carbon footprint and our dependence on fossil fuels.[1] The main roadblock towards the commercialization of this technology is the absence of a sustainable catalytic
system. To comply with the sustainable chemistry principles, this system has to employ low-toxicity or nontoxic earth-abun-
dant materials as catalysts and water as a solvent, while oper-
ating at mild conditions (atmospheric CO2 pressures and near room temperatures).
Unfortunately, among the metals that are sufficiently active in CO2 electroreduction, [1c, 2] only Sn and Cu meet the sustainable chemistry criteria. Tin is “specialized” in the synthesis of formate, owing to its inability to dissociate the C¢O bonds. Copper is unique, as it can synthetize C1+ hydrocarbons and oxygenates such as ethylene, ethane, ethanol, and propanol.[2]
However, the performance of these two metals is plagued by large overpotentials (ca. ¢1 V), fast deactivation, and, in the case of Cu, low selectivity.[3] The large overpotentials and low
selectivity emanate from the thermodynamic and kinetic challenges of CO2 reduction. [1a] The fast deactivation is mostly caused by electrode poisoning from heavy-metal contaminants, which are typical of conventional electrolytes.[4] In addition, the electrode surface can be modified by cathodic corrosion, such as dissolution/re-precipitation[5] and poisoned by reaction products such as carbon,[3c] which is poorly understood.
Although the robustness of the electrocatalyst is as important as its energy efficiency1 and current density, prior research efforts have mainly focused on the improvement of the latter
two properties. The main design principles implemented so far in this area include (nano)structuring and/or oxidation of metal surfaces.[6] Although this approach has proven to be very efficient, it is intrinsically incapable of protecting the electrodes
from deactivation by heavy metals and corrosion, and a miti-
gating technique such as addition of water-soluble chelating agents to the electrolyte does not work for copper.[4]
In this context, it is critical to develop a new class of material that is, by design, more robust and catalytically active than
metals. Such an emerging class includes materials based on Ndoped sp2 carbon, including N-heteroaromatic organic compounds and N-doped graphitic carbon.[3d, 7] In fact, N-doped carbon nanotubes (N-CNTs)[8] are only marginally inferior in formate synthesis to nano-Sn on graphene.[6a] Much lower overpotentials of approximately ¢0.35 V are required to produce formate through electropolymerized phthalocyanine com-
plexes of Ni and Co, although the faradaic efficiencies of these electrocatalysts is unclear.[9] Electropolymerized pyridine com-
plexes of Cr, Co, and Fe convert CO2 to formaldehyde in 0.1 m NaClO4 at ¢1.1 V (Ag/AgCl) with faradaic efficiencies of 87, 39, and 28 %, respectively.[10] Interestingly, water-soluble N-hetero-
cycles and N-heterocycle-based ionic liquids stabilize Sn electrodes, with increasing current density and decreasing overpotential in the formate synthesis.[3a, 11]
Given these data, along with the well-documented catalytic
activity of metal complexes of macrocycles with pyridyl ligands,[3c, 12] we were curious to test the effect of N-heteroaromatic polymers on the catalytic activity of metals. These poly-
mers have not yet been employed as a building block in CO2 electrocatalysts. The exception is the incorporation of cobalt
The development of efficient and robust catalysts based on earth-abundant and nontoxic materials is critical for the viabili-
ty of the electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 into useful chemicals. Herein, we report a new class of electrocatalysts with incorporated mechanisms of their stabilization. A Cu electrode
coated with a poly(4-vinyl pyridine) film synthesizes formate at a faradaic efficiency of 40 % at an overpotential of ¢0.67 V, and its catalytic activity does not degrade after 30 h of operation.
We attribute the outstanding catalytic properties of the new hybrid material to the formation of Cu–polymer complexes, as
well as to new intrinsic mechanisms of the electrode stabiliza-
tion offered by the N-heteroaromatic polymer. This is the first report of CO2 electroreduction with copper–N-heteroaromatic ligand complexes. More generally, our study offers a new simple strategy to design and prepare robust CO2 reduction electrocatalysts based on earth-abundant metals.

phthalocyanine complexes in a poly(4-vinylpyridine) membrane coated on a graphite electrode, which significantly increases the selectivity of the complexes to CO versus H2. [13] At the same time, polyvinyl pyridines have already gained impor-
tance as catalysts of gas-phase reactions and have promising physicochemical properties.[14] In particular, CuII complexes of poly(4-vinyl pyridine) (P4VP) (Scheme 1) are catalytically active
in the water-gas shift reaction[15] and dehydrogenation of ethylene.[14a] The mesoporous structure of P4VP allows easy diffu-
sion of small molecules and anions through the polymeric network.[14b, 16] It is also known that P4VP functions as a proton-exchanging membrane.[13] The pKa of P4VP is in the 3.8–4.5 range.[17] The permeability and proton conductivity of P4VP is important for mass transport. In P4VP complexes with copper,
the copper cations can coordinate with several pyridyl groups, including groups from different polymer chains, which increases the rigidity and insolubility of the polymer matrix.[14a, 15, 16b, 18]
Coordination to metals induces cross-linking of the polymer, leading to its semiconducting-to-metallic conductivity[19] and anticorrosion properties.[16b, 20]
The synthesis of renewable formate HCOO¢ (or formic acid HCOOH) is among the most significant technological targets with one of the highest chances to be realized.[1a, 3b, 21] Indeed,
CO2 conversion to formate [Eq. (1)] is the simplest CO2 reduction reaction, as it involves only two proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps and no dissociation of the C¢O bond or formation of the C¢C bond:
CO2 þ 2 Hþ þ 2 e¢ ! HCOOH E0 ¼ ¢0:225 V vs: SHE, at pH 0, 1 atm CO2, and 25 C½22¤
ð1Þ
Moreover, formic acid is an expensive feedstock (1000– 1700$ t¢1) with a growing demand from the agriculture, leather, textile, rubber, chemical, and pharmaceuticals sectors. This chemical is also of interest as a fuel for low-temperature fuel cells[23] and as a carrier for hydrogen storage.[24]
Herein, we discover that coating a copper electrode with
a micron-thick film of P4VP promotes its activity in formate synthesis, and it suppresses the synthesis of other carbona-
ceous products, except for 1–5 % CO. More importantly, this modification renders a superior robustness to the electrode.
On the basis of Raman, XPS, and cyclic voltammetry data, as well as the catalytic activity of the P4VP films on copper and
carbon, we explain these findings in terms of the semi-permeability and complexing properties of the polymer coatings,
which result in the formation of catalytically active copper–pyridyl complexes.

sections.heading: 2.1. Catalytic Performance
sections.text:
We start with analysis of the energy efficiency of the P4VP-
coated Cu electrode (henceforth denoted P4VP/Cu) followed by comparison with that of the uncoated Cu electrodes. P4VP/
Cu synthesizes only formate in the liquid phase, with a maximum faradaic efficiency of 40 3 % at ¢1.3 V (Ag/AgCl) (Figure 1). Given that the formal potential (E0) of the reaction in Equation (2) at pH 6.8 is ¢0.63 V (Ag/AgCl), the overpotential of the maximum efficiency is only ¢0.67 V. Analysis of the gas-phase products detected only hydrogen (from reduction of water) and small amounts (1–5 %) of CO.
A comparison with polycrystalline Cu shows that the polymer coating significantly promotes formate synthesis (Figure 1 a). Uncoated Cu achieves a maximum faradaic efficiency of only 13 % between ¢1.4 and ¢1.6 V. A slightly higher faradaic efficiency of 20–25 % in the same potential range has

been reported for polycrystalline Cu electrodes prepared by electrochemical polishing.[25] As seen in Table S1, P4VP/Cu is
also superior to the more advanced, surface-structured copper electrodes, except for the Cu2O-derived electrodes reported by Li and Kanan.[26] In addition, in contrast to the uncoated copper electrodes, P4VP/Cu almost fully lacks the capacity to
push CO2 reduction beyond formate, as the only other carbonaceous product is 1–5 % CO. This fact is consistent with the switch of the catalytic sites from metallic copper to copper–
polymer complexes (vide infra). In terms of current density, P4VP/Cu is comparable with nano-Cu supported by carbon,[27]
but inferior to the structured Cu electrodes listed in Table S1, which is expected given the higher conductivity of metals.
It is also instructive to compare P4VP/Cu with the best earth-abundant electrocatalysts reported for formate so far. As
seen in Table S1, P4VP/Cu is more energy efficient in formate synthesis at overpotentials approximately ¢0.7 V more than Ndoped CNTs[8] and nano-Bi,[28] and as efficient as nano-Sn on carbon.[6a] At more cathodic potentials, the P4VP/Cu electrode is inferior to N-CNTs, nano-Bi, and nano-Sn, owing to a shift in
its selectivity toward the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). To elucidate the nature of the promoting effects of the poly-
mer film at low overpotentials, we compare the catalytic activi-
ty of P4VP/Cu with that of P4VP on carbon (P4VP/C). As seen from Figure 1 b, P4VP/C is much less effective than P4VP/Cu in
formate synthesis, and there is no significant difference in the efficiency of P4VP/C and carbon alone. In contrast, the P4VP/C electrode soaked in a CuII salt solution produces formate in a similar manner to P4VP/Cu; although, the composition of
other products is different (the data are not shown as this
study is in progress). Therefore, it is not the polymer itself that catalyzes the reaction at P4VP/Cu, but rather Cu–P4VP com-
plexes. This conclusion was confirmed by using XPS and Raman analyses (vide infra).
Another key result is that the polymer renders outstanding catalytic stability to the P4VP/Cu electrode. In fact, except for
the first 10–20 min of the first electrolysis test (not shown), the
average cathodic current at P4VP/Cu is constant or slowly increasing (Figure 2). The increase in current can be related to
the formation of new catalytic sites caused by the slow background corrosion of the copper support. This interpretation is supported by the slow increase in the surface concentration of copper in the polymer film after the first electrolysis test (see XPS results below), as well as by the slow appearance of
a blackish hue in the electrode color (Figure S3, SI). Importantly, the corrosion of the copper support does not
have a statistically significant impact on the formate selectivity of P4VP/Cu (Figure 1 a). After approximately 30 h of operation at potentials between ¢1.0 and ¢1.5 V, its catalytic activity was reproduced within 10 %. For comparison, the best report-
ed stability of uncovered surface-structured copper electrodes in a more pure (99.99 %) bicarbonate electrolyte is limited to 6 h,[29] whereas the stability of (nano)structured Cu electrodes
in ultrapure (>99.9999 %) bicarbonate has been reported for 7 h.[26] The stability of the catalytic current at nano-Sn and
nano-Bi (in KHCO3 of non-disclosed purity) has been reported for 18 and 7 h, respectively.[8, 28]
The robustness of P4VP/Cu was confirmed by using SEM and spectroscopic analyses. Namely, SEM reveals no cracks or
peeling of the polymer coating (Figure 3). However, electrolysis
changes the macromorphology, as evidenced by the appear-

sections.heading: 2.2. XPS Characterization
sections.text:
The XPS spectra of freshly fabricated P4VP/Cu electrodes
(Figure 4, top row) are similar to the reported spectra of P4VP:[30] The N 1s peak presents a singlet at 399.3 0.1 eV at the same binding energy observed for the bulk polymer.[30]
After electrolysis, a second N 1s state develops at 400.3 eV (Fig-
ure 4 a’), in concert with an increase of the atomic Cu concentration (Table 1). This new state has a similar binding energy as that in copper–pyridyl complexes formed with P4VP,[15] sug-
gesting that these complexes are also formed under the electrolysis conditions. The relative intensity of the N 1s signal at 400.3 eV varies in a 7–11 % range (Table 1). The fact that about 90 % of the pyridyl groups remain free follows the “all-or-noth-
ing” feature observed for the P4VP interaction with CuII.[16b] Namely, the appearance of the first CuII–polymer complex facil-
itates consecutive complexations along the chain, resulting in the simultaneous presence of extremely loaded and nearly un-
loaded polymer chains. The low loading of Cu also indicates that the Cu–P4VP complexes are formed with a low local con-
centration of copper cations dissolved in the polymer. Interestingly, the Cu 2p signal is already detected in the XPS
spectra of the as-fabricated P4VP/Cu electrode (Figure 4 b and
Table 1). This signal increases by 50 % after 5 h of electrolysis at ¢1.2 V, and then by 30 % after the following 25 h of electrolysis at different potentials. Hence, the polymer is mostly loaded with copper during the soaking of P4VP/Cu in 0.1 m KHCO3 and during the first electrolysis. The slow increase in current under potentiostatic conditions (Figure 2) can be related to
the in situ formation of these complexes. On the basis of vol-
tammetric data (Figure S5), we explain the formation of copper–P4VP complexes during the soaking step by the
anodic corrosion of copper at the open-circuit potential (ca. 0 V). Complex formation during CO2 reduction is attributed copper corrosion under the electrolysis conditions. The XPS data are ambiguous regarding the oxidation state
of the coordinated copper cations, owing to the invasive
nature of these measurements. The Cu 2p3/2 peak shifted from 933.4 to 932.4 eV, whereas the intensity of the shakeup satel-
lite at 942 eV decreased during the 4 h measurements. Given that CuII is characterized by the Cu 2p3/2 peak at 934 eV and the strong satellite at 942 eV,[31] this picture indicates reduction of incorporated cupric cations. In the resulting spectrum (Fig-
ure 4 b’), the Cu 2p3/2 peak is at 932.4 eV, which indicates the dominance of either the CuI or Cu0. The persistence of the satellite testifies that there is still an admixture of CuII in the air-
exposed polymer film. Hence, the oxidation state of the coordinated copper under ambient conditions is likely to be dominated by CuII. It is worth emphasizing the importance of the oxidation and coordination state of copper under the CO2 reduction conditions, which can only be identified by using
in situ methods such as XANES. The electrolysis has almost no effect on the atomic concen-
trations and core-level spectra of carbon (Table 1), which indicates the chemical stability of the polymer. The C 1s spectrum
ChemElectroChem 2016, 3, 74 – 82 www.chemelectrochem.org Ó 2016 Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim77
lacks a carbonate or carboxylate state at 288–289 eV,[32] suggesting that coordinated carbonate ligands, if any, are unstable
under the XPS conditions.

sections.heading: 2.3. Raman Spectroscopy
sections.text:
The Raman spectra of an as-fabricated P4VP/Cu electrode and
the same electrode after 1 and 30 h of electrolysis are very similar to the spectrum of P4VP (Figure 5), which provides addi-
tional evidence for the chemical robustness of P4VP/Cu. The exception is the presence of a strong peak at 620 cm¢1 in the spectra of the electrodes, owing to the contribution from the copper oxide layer at the Cu–polymer interface.[33] The assignment of the polymer peaks can be found elsewhere.[34] For analysis of the complex formation of interest are peaks at 993 and 1598 cm¢1, which are attributed to in-plane symmetric and asymmetric ring deformations, labeled n1 and n8a, respectively. These modes are most sensitive to the s-coordination of pyridyl groups.[14a, 18–19, 35]
At the same time, the Raman spectra of the P4VP/Cu elec-
trode exhibit small additional features that point to the forma-
tion of copper–polymer complexes (Figure 5). First of all, the used electrode is characterized by a weak shoulder at 260– 270 cm¢1 (shown in the insert), which can be assigned to the Cu¢N bonds revealed by XPS. In fact, a broad peak at approximately 250 cm¢1 is typical of the Raman spectra for CuCl2–
P4VP complexes.[36] A spectral range of 200–270 cm¢1 has been reported for the Cu–N stretching mode of pyridine complexes with CuII.[37] The low intensity of the Cu–N peak is consistent with the low (7–11 %) fraction of the bound nitrogen atoms. Secondly, shoulders at 1025 and 1615–1620 cm¢1 appear and develop with time. These shoulders are at the same positions as the n1 and n8a ring stretching modes of Cu II–P4VP complexes.[14a, 18–19, 35] The blueshift of these peaks is caused by electron polarization upon the pyridyl–copper s coordination and correlates with the strength of the N–metal bond.[38] The low relative intensity of the shoulders reflects the fact that the majority of the pyridyl groups is not involved in the complexation. Finally, there is a change in the relative intensity of the polymer backbone peaks in the 1300–1580 cm¢1 range, which can be related to the reorganization of the polymer chains. This
effect is typical of complex formation between linear organic polymers and metal cations.[16b]
Thus, the Raman spectra support the XPS-based conclusions about the in situ formation of CuII–P4VP complexes. It is the first report of formate synthesis from copper–N-heteroaromatic
ligand complexes to date. Among the complexes of earthabundant metals, only poly-phthalocyanines of Ni and Co,[9] and copper rubeanate metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)[39]
have been known to electrocatalyze CO2 conversion to formate in water. In addition, Raman spectroscopy confirms that the
polymer is chemically stable under the reaction conditions, al-
ChemElectroChem 2016, 3, 74 – 82 www.chemelectrochem.org Ó 2016 Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim78
though there is reorganization of the polymer chains assigned to the complex formation.
Finally, voltammetric analysis of P4VP/Cu and Cu electrodes (Figure S5) reveals that copper–P4VP complexes are formed through anodic corrosion of copper electrodes at ¢0.3–0 V, which is in agreement with an earlier report.[20] This explains
the appearance of copper at the polymer surface after soaking the freshly deposited P4VP/Cu electrode in 0.1 m KHCO3. In addition, voltammograms show that CuII in the oxidized form of the Cu–P4VP complexes are more electronegative than CuII in the anodic corrosion products of uncoated copper. Moreover, the reduced form of the CuII–P4VP complexes interacts more strongly with CO2/HCO3
¢ than copper metal, which leads to the suppression of the HER at P4VP/Cu as compared to Cu.

sections.heading: 3. Discussion
sections.text:
Mainstream research towards the development of a sustainable
catalyst for CO2 electroreduction has focused, so far, on increasing the energy and current efficiency, whereas much less
attention has been paid to the robustness. We have shown
that a hybrid electrode prepared by coating a copper electrode with P4VP is an effective and robust electrocatalyst for
CO2 conversion to formate. Below, we offer our interpretation of the promoting effect of the polymer.
We relate the significant change in the catalytic activity of Cu to the formation of copper–polymer complexes, as ob-
served by using XPS and Raman spectroscopy. Indeed, these
complexes are expected to have a narrower structure distribution than the catalytic sites on metallic copper. Moreover, the
carbon–carbon coupling is precluded in monocenter complexes, as this reaction requires close proximity of two co-adsorbed CO2 adducts. [40] The low yield of CO points to the suppressed capacity of the complexes to dissociate the C¢O bond. The still high selectivity of P4VP/Cu for the HER can be ex-
plained by the low (7–11 %) doping level of the polymer by copper. As a result, the majority of pyridyl groups are accessi-
ble for the HER. The catalytic activity of pyridyl groups in the HER is known from literature.[41] Hence, we believe that further
optimization of the doping level and the electrolyte (pH, composition, and concentration), along with the employment of
a gas-diffusion electrode, can help suppress the HER and increase the formate yield.
Catalysis with Cu–P4VP complexes also explains the lower overpotential of formate synthesis when using P4VP/Cu compared to metallic Cu. These complexes interact more strongly with CO2/HCO3 ¢ and are more electronegative than the catalytic sites on metallic Cu; the reason is the dative binding from
the nitrogen lone pair to the metal, where the pyridyl group and metal acquire positive and negative charge, respectively.[42] The Cu0–P4VP and CuI–P4VP complexes have metal-based
redox activity, because their highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) is located on the central atom.[42] As a result, the ionization energy of copper in the Cu0–pyridine complex is lower by 2.3 eV compared to Cu,[42] which makes the former a stronger reductant. Moreover, CuI–P4VP complexes are more electronegative than Cu2O nanoparticles dispersed on zeolites and
oxides, as the former donate a higher electron density to the CO ligand than the latter.[14a] The higher electronegativity of the Cu0–P4VP and CuI–P4VP complexes may be the reason for the relatively low overpotential of formate synthesis at the
P4VP/Cu electrode compared to uncoated Cu. According to the XPS results (Table 1), only 1 % of the pyridyl
groups at the polymer surface are coordinated by copper after the electrode preparation. We explain the appearance of the
Cu–P4VP complexes as anodic corrosion of the copper support
during the soaking step. Interestingly, the concentration of coordinated pyridyl groups abruptly increases to 7 % after 1 h of electrolysis at ¢1.6 V, and then increases to 11 % over the following 29 h of electrolysis at different potentials (Table 1).
Hence, the formation of Cu–P4VP complexes can be associated with cathodic corrosion of the copper support under the CO2 reduction conditions. We are the first to report the formation
of Cu–P4VP complexes under the CO2 reduction conditions. The discovered cathodic pathway of complex formation can
be used to prepare other catalytically active metal complexes with polyvinylpyridines.
The above results indicate that the cathodic corrosion of the copper support during CO2 reduction (the so-called anomalous dissolution) is instrumental for the catalytic activity of P4VP/
Cu. Although the exact mechanism of this effect is unknown, it is likely to have the same ligand-promoted origin as the cathodic corrosion of copper during oxygen reduction,[43] as well as the copper alloying upon cathodic electrodeposition of metals on copper.[44] Namely, copper cathodes dissolve when the attacking oxidant forms strong charge-transfer complexes with
copper. These complexes are ejected into the electrical double
layer and are further reduced at the cathode. The resulting leaching/re-precipitation process roughens the cathode surface.[5] In the presence of a P4VP overlayer, however, the ejected copper species are immobilized by the pyridyl ligands.
Once formed, the Cu–P4VP complexes partially inhibit further corrosion of the copper support. The inhibition effect can be
related to the higher rigidity and reduced permeability of the metal cross-linked polymer,[14a, 15, 16b, 18] which has already been employed to protect copper electrodes from anodic corrosion.[20] The barrier properties of Cu–P4VP complexes also explain the observed prevalence (ca. 90 %) of non-coordinated
pyridyl groups at the polymer surface after 30 h. This indicates that the copper–polymer complexes are formed at a low local
concentration of copper cations dissolved in the polymer. The polymer film not only improves the catalytic activity of
copper in formate synthesis, but also provides important
mechanisms for electrode stabilization (Scheme 2). Firstly, the catalytic stability is provided by the relatively uniform struc-
tures of the Cu–P4VP complexes formed upon anomalous dissolution of copper. In contrast, the catalytic sites on uncovered
copper electrodes are continuously modified by dissolution/reprecipitation,[5] which degrades their selectivity.[26] The second mechanism is the stabilizing role of the bulky polymer coils,
which can preclude the modification of Cu–P4VP complexes, for example, by aggregation of their central atoms. The third
mechanism relates to the presence of approximately 90 % of non-complexed pyridyl groups at the P4VP/Cu surface. These
ChemElectroChem 2016, 3, 74 – 82 www.chemelectrochem.org Ó 2016 Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim79
groups have a high affinity for heavy metals,[16b] and hence can immobilize them, thereby preventing poisoning of the Cu–
P4VP complexes. In fact, the survey XPS spectra of the heavily
used P4VP/Cu electrode show the presence of traces of Pb and Cr on the electrode surface (Figure S5). Hence, the non-com-
plexed groups can act as a sink for intrinsic heavy-metal contaminants of standard-purity (99.7 + %) electrolytes, thereby
making the electrode tolerant to these contaminants. In contrast, metal electrodes are quickly deactivated in non-purified electrolytes.[3a, 45]
Although further studies, especially those employing in situ spectroscopic methods such as XANES, EPR, and vibrational spectroscopy, are required to elucidate the exact structure of the Cu–P4VP complexes and the oxidation state of Cu under
the catalytic conditions, the available data allow us to conclude that CuI–P4VP complexes are able to bind CO2 because they have ‘empty’ (weakly coordinated to the solvent) coordination sites.[14a] Moreover, in general, the progressive hardening of the polymer network by the coordinated metal cations increases the coordinative unsaturation of these cations.[16b] Finally, the co-production of CO argues that the Cu–P4VP complexes synthesize formate through the carboxyl ¢COOH route, because the alternative formate¢OCHO route is unable to produce CO.[46] Indirect support of this conclusion is provided by
the catalytic activity of CuCl2–P4VP complexes in the water-gas shift reaction.[15]
Thus, the discovered polymer–metal architecture (Scheme 2) employs the main advantages of homogeneous electrocata-
lysts such as high selectivity and low overpotential and has a superior robustness compared to metal electrodes. These
promoting effects are explained by the multifunctional roles of the polymer film. It 1) switches the catalytic activity from the
Cu surface to Cu–polymer complexes; 2) increases the affinity of these complexes for CO2/HCO3
¢ , as compared to metallic Cu; 3) stabilizes the catalytic sites; 4) partially inhibits cathodic corrosion of the copper support, while converting the dis-
solved copper species into new catalytic sites with the same selectivity; and 5) serves as a sink for heavy-metal contaminants. In addition, as proposed by Kaneko and co-workers for
cobalt phthalocyanine complexes incorporated in P4VP, noncoordinated pendant pyridyl groups can contribute to the pro-
tonation–deprotonation steps and create microenvironments that are beneficial for CO2 reduction. [13] Another advantage of the new polymer-coated metal electrode is that it is easy to fabricate and does not include expensive components (e.g.
precious metals, enzymes, or macrocycles).

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
Herein, we have discovered a new class of earth-abundant electrocatalysts, which have intrinsic mechanisms for the stabi-
lization of their catalytic sites. We have shown that P4VP doped with Cu, owing to corrosion of the copper support, is
an effective and robust electrocatalyst for CO2 conversion to formate. We are the first to demonstrate the electrocatalytic of Cu–pyridyl complexes in CO2 conversion to formate in water.
The energy efficiency of P4VP/Cu is better than or comparable to that of earlier reported micro- and nanostructured copper electrodes and copper rubeanate MOFs (Table S1). Although the P4VP/Cu electrode is inferior to the metallic Cu electrodes in terms of current density, it is superior in terms of
robustness. The catalytic activity of P4VP/Cu does not degrade after 30 h of operation in a non-purified (>99.7 %) bicarbonate solution. This electrode can easily be prepared by corrosion of polymer-coated metals and does not include expensive components such as precious metals, enzymes, or macrocycles. We are the first to demonstrate the in situ formation of metal–
polymer complexes at the metal–polymer interface under CO2 reduction conditions, which can be a new strategy for the fabrication of catalytically active metal–polymer complexes.
Our results encourage further search for the best earthabundant electrocatalyst among polymer–metal structures
through 1) varying the metal and the doping level, 2) manipulating the operation conditions (e.g. pH and electrolyte), 3) em-
ploying a gas-diffusion-electrode cell to increase the current
density, and 4) modifying the polymer structure by isomerization of the pyridyl groups, chemical cross-linking, and grafting
of other functional groups.

sections.heading: Experimental Section
sections.text:
Solutions were prepared by using KHCO3 (Fisher, ACS certified, >99.7 %). According to the manufacturer’s specifications, KHCO3 contains a maximum of 5 ppm Fe and 5 ppm heavy metals. In all cases, Barnsted Nanopure water was used with a resistivity of 18.2 MW cm and a total organic carbon content no higher than

3 ppb. All glassware was washed in a Piranha solution [1:3 H2O2(30 %): H2SO4] and rinsed several times with Nanopure water.

sections.heading: Preparation of Electrodes
sections.text:
We chose linear P4VP (MW = 60 000, Sigma Aldrich) because of its higher solubility (soluble in highly acidic solutions and organic solvents) compared to the cross-linked counterpart. Also, linear polymers have higher backbone flexibility, which can facilitate the favorable arrangement of pyridyl groups around the reagents and intermediates of the catalytic reaction.
The polymer films were prepared by coating a copper foil (0.5 mm thick, 99.9985 % (metals basis) [Alfa Aesar (catalog number 11392)] and a carbon rod (3 mm diameter Õ 30 m, 99.999 %) [Strem Chemicals, UK (catalog number 930605)] . The surfaces of these supports were prepared by grinding with a 400 grit silicon carbide paper followed by ultrasonication to detach leftover abrasive particles from the surface. The Cu and C electrodes were further washed in dichloromethane (99.8 + %, Acros Organics), air dried, and dipcoated with P4VP by immersing the electrode in a 100 mg mL¢1 polymer solution in dichloromethane for 60 s and slow (0.5 mm s¢1) withdrawal. The thickness of the resulting P4VP films on Cu was 2 1 mm, as estimated by using ellipsometry (a-SE, J. A. Woollam Co.). The polymer-coated electrode was air-dried and soaked in 0.1 m KHCO3 for 2–3 h to remove residual dichloromethane and to form CuII–polymer complexes. Afterwards, to protect the polymer coating from dissolution during electrolysis, the electrode was dipped for 1 s in a 0.1 % Nafion solution (water diluted 5 % Nafion solution from Aldrich) and dried overnight.

sections.heading: Controlled-Potential Electrolysis
sections.text:
Preparative electrolysis was performed at constant potential (¢0.8 to ¢2.2 V) under stirring conditions (1500 rpm). For this purpose, we used a custom-made electrolysis cell (Ace glass) with two compartments that were separated by a Nafion membrane (Nafion 117, thickness 0.007’’, Aldrich) and sealed with septa caps. The reference electrode was an Ag/AgCl electrode (RE-5B, BASi). The counter electrode was a roughened Pt foil. The anolyte was either 0.1 m KHCO3 or 0.1 m K2SO4. The immersed surface area of the working electrodes was 5.0 0.1 cm2. The catholyte was 5 or 7 mL of 0.1 m KHCO3 saturated with 1 atm CO2 (Lasershield grade, TechAir). The headspace in the working electrode compartment was 20 or 22 mL.
Before each of the CO2 reduction experiments, the catholyte solution was saturated by bubbling CO2 for at least 30 min. Afterwards, the electrodes were subjected to 5–6 CV cycles at 50 mV s¢1 from 0 to ¢1.6 V in the electrolysis cell to monitor the reproducibility of their initial state. During the electrolysis, we continuously bubbled CO2 at 30–40 mL min
¢1 through the electrolyte. In this case, the pH value after electrolysis was the same as the initial value of 6.8. To probe the gas-phase products, we repeated the experiments under the sealed conditions. In this case, the pH increased to 6.9–7.0. Depending on the potential, the current density on P4VP/Cu ranged from 0.1 to 5 mA cm¢2. The accumulated total charge was kept in the 5–10 C range in all the cases. As a control, we also ran electrolysis at P4VP/Cu at ¢1.2 V in N2-saturated 0.1 m K2SO4 with an initial pH value of 6.8, and did not detect any CO2 reduction products.
To characterize the robustness of the prepared P4VP/Cu electrode, we reused it for electrolysis at all of the potentials reported, and duplicate measurements were conducted with a freshly prepared
electrode. To exclude the possible effect of aging on the electrode activity, the electrolysis potential was selected randomly in both the initial and duplicate sets of the experiments. In contrast, the Cu and C electrodes were freshly prepared for each electrolysis experiment.

sections.heading: Characterization of Electrolysis Products
sections.text:
Liquid products of CO2 reduction were identified and quantified by using 1H NMR spectroscopy (Bruker Avance 500 MHz) with water suppression through an excitation sculpting-pulse method. After the electrolysis, the catholyte was diluted with D2O at a ratio of 9:1. D2O contained 0.75 w % of trimethylsilyl propanoic acid (the solution was supplied by Aldrich) as an internal standard. The amount of each product was quantified by comparing the integrated peak area of the internal standard with that of the products. The sensitivity of this method towards formate was estimated as >0.5 ppm (Figure S1).
Gaseous products were analyzed by using a micro-GC (GC = gas chromatograph; Inficon, GC 3000 A) and GC–MS (Agilent 6890). The micro-GC instrument was fitted with four columns. A Molsieve column was used to separate and detect H2, CH4, and CO gases, whereas a PLOT U column was used for CO2 and OV-1 as well as alumina columns were used to separate light hydrocarbons and olefins. The GC–MS instrument was fitted with a PLOT Q column. The inlet temperature was kept at 120 8C. The mass spectrometer and NIST Standard Reference Database 1A were used to analyze the separated products. For the analysis, 2 mL of the headspace gases was collected after electrolysis under the sealed conditions and injected into the micro-GC inlet through a headspace sampler (Dani Instruments, HSS 86.50). The GC instruments were calibrated by injecting 2 mL of calibration gas mixtures that had been prepared in gas bags.

sections.heading: Characterization of Electrodes
sections.text:
The polymer films, both the initial films and those obtained after electrolysis, were characterized by using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and cyclic voltammetry (CV).
SEM images were obtained by using a 4700-Hitachi SEM microscope with a voltage of 0.6 kV and a current at 20 mA.
Raman spectra of the polymer films were acquired by using a LABRAM-ARAMIS confocal Raman microscope with a 50 Õ objective and a diffraction grating of 1200 grooves mm¢1. As the excitation source, a 17 mW 633 nm HeNe laser was used without attenuation by a filter. The monochromator was calibrated before each set of measurements by using the zero-order peak and the Si peak at 520.7 cm¢1 of a Si-wafer reference sample.
XPS specra were collected with a PerkinElmer PHI 5500 instrument by using a monochromatic AlKa source (1486.6 eV) with a pass energy of 17.6 eV, at a takeoff angle of 458 and pressures of approximately 10¢10 Torr. The multiplex spectra were collected at 0.05 eV steps over 4 h. A low-energy electron flood gun was employed for charge neutralization. The binding energy was corrected by shifting the center of the polymer C 1s peak, which is attributed to aromatic carbon, to 285.5 eV. In this case, the C 1s peak of saturated (sp3) hydrocarbons is at 285 eV.[30] Spectra were curve-fitted with 80 % Gaussian + 20 % Lorentzian peaks, using AugerScan 4.0 software and PHI atomic sensitivity factors. The full width at half maximum values of the N 1s, O 1s, and C 1s peaks in the curve fit-
